texts.title: Questionnaire
texts.html:
Respondents complete the background information questionnaire in English, French, German, Japanese, or Korean. For brevity, we display only the English version here. The shaded boxes are not part of the questionnaire. They point to the figures in Online Appendix A.2 that report the responses.

  1. 1.

    Where do you live?
    Choose one of the following answers (shown in a drop-down list).

    • Australia
    • Canada
    • France
    • Germany
    • India
    • Japan
    • Singapore
    • South Korea
    • United Kingdom
    • United States
    • Other
  2. 2.
    How old are you?
    Choose one of the following answers (shown in a drop-down list).

    • Under 21
    • 21–24
    • 25–34
    • 35–44
    • 45–54
    • 55–64
    • 65+

    Responses: Figure A1, Panel (a)

  3. 3.
    What is your gender?
    Choose one of the following answers.
    If you choose “Prefer to self-describe:” please also specify your choice in the accompanying text field.

    • Male
    • Female
    • Prefer to self-describe:

    Responses: Figure A1, Panel (b)

  4. 4.
    What is the highest qualification you have completed?
    If you are currently studying, please indicate the highest degree you have already received.
    Choose one of the following answers.
    If you choose “Other:” please also specify your choice in the accompanying text field.

    • No degree
    • School diploma / Apprenticeship
    • Bachelor’s degree (or equivalent)
    • Master’s degree (MBA, MA, MSc, or equivalent)
    • Doctorate (PhD or equivalent)
    • Other:

    Responses: Figure A1, Panel (c)

  5. 5.
    Which of the following investment types do you currently have money allocated to, either individually or jointly with someone else?
    Note: Only include investments you made yourself or directly instructed a third party to make for you (e.g., a financial advisor). Select all that apply.

    • Individual stocks (publicly traded equity)
    • Mutual funds or exchange-traded funds (ETFs)
    • Derivatives (Options, Futures, or Forwards)
    • Cryptocurrencies
    • None of the above

    Responses: Figure A2, Panel (a)

  6. 6.

    Approximately how much is your current total investable assets, in US Dollars?
    (You may use xe.com to convert from your local currency to US dollars)
    Please include in your approximation:

    • Cash on hand and in bank accounts
    • Investments in stocks, mutual funds, ETFs, derivatives, and cryptocurrencies

    Please exclude in your approximation:

    • Non-investment assets (e.g. your home, vehicles, collectibles)

    Your response will be kept completely confidential.
    Choose one of the following answers (shown in a drop-down list).

    • Less than $1,000
    • $1,000 to $9,999
    • $10,000 to $24,999
    • $25,000 to $49,999
    • $50,000 to $99,999
    • $100,000 to $249,999
    • $250,000 to $499,999
    • $500,000 to $999,999
    • $1m+
    • Prefer not to answer

    Responses: Figure A2, Panel (b)

  7. 7.
    Approximately how often do you make changes to any of the above investment types?
    This could be a change to the amount invested or a change in investment type
    Choose one of the following answers

    • Less often than once a year
    • Once a year
    • Once every few months/quarterly
    • Once a month
    • Once a week or more often

    Responses: Figure A2, Panel (c)

  8. 8.
    Please indicate the primary sources from which your current wealth has been accumulated.
    Choose one of the following answers.
    If you choose “Other” please also specify your choice in the accompanying text field.

    • Employment income (working for an employer)
    • Business ownership or self-employment income
    • Inheritance or significant financial gifts from family/other
    • Proceeds from selling a significant personal asset (e.g., primary residence, valuable collectibles)
    • Other:

    Responses: Figure A2, Panel (d)

  9. 9.
    How would you describe your level of investment knowledge?
    Choose one of the following answers.

    • Complete beginner – I have little to no knowledge of investing
    • Rudimentary
    • Intermediate
    • Advanced
    • Expert – I have professional-level knowledge or significant personal experience in investing

    Responses: Figure A3, Panel (a)

  10. 10.
    Which of the following statements comes closest to the amount of financial risk that you are willing to take when you save or make investments?
    Choose one of the following answers.

    • Not willing to take any financial risks
    • Take average financial risks expecting to earn average returns
    • Take above-average financial risks expecting to earn above-average returns
    • Take substantial risk expecting to earn substantial returns

    Responses: Figure A3, Panel (b)

head.title: Prompting the AI Interviewer
head.html:
We construct a prompt for the GPT model to simulate a one-on-one interview in which a finance researcher examines an individual’s decisions to invest in specific stocks.1 The prompt follows best practice in prompt design at the time of development and combines role-play, chain-of-thought prompting, zero-shot reasoning, few-shot examples, strategic reasoning, instruction following, and self-consistency in an agentic workflow.2 We summarize the prompt below.

  1. 1.
    Persona and Role. We first define the persona of a finance researcher who interviews individuals about their decisions to invest in particular stocks. This persona guides the tone, conduct, and reasoning of the GPT model’s responses.3 It specifies the interviewer’s identity (finance professor), demeanor, communication style, task, goal, and preferred language.
  2. 2.
    Core Objective. We then state the objective of the interview, which is to understand how individuals select specific stocks. head.title: Prompts for the Post-interview Analysis
head.html: We construct six prompts corresponding to the four stages of the post-interview analysis described in Section 3.3 of the main paper.5 We use three prompts to construct the argument maps, one for bottom-up mechanism generation, and two for validation and refinement. The final scoring stage reuses the validation prompt and requires no separate prompt (Online Appendix C.3.3). This section summarizes the key elements of these prompts. Throughout this section, we retain the label “mechanism” that the prompts themselves use for the recurrent decision rules. The main paper refers to these rules as heuristics (Section 3.3). We use prompting techniques similar to those in Online Appendix B and, for brevity, do not describe the components that repeat them.

texts.html:
This stage uses three prompts, which (i) generate a directed acyclic graph (DAG) for each transcript, (ii) standardize and aggregate the nodes independently generated from the 1,540 transcripts, and (iii) map the original node names to the standardized set. Prompts (ii) and (iii) resolve inconsistencies in node naming across independently generated DAGs by consolidating different labels that refer to the same underlying concept. The final output is 1,540 DAGs whose node names are fully standardized across all transcripts.

C.1.1 Generating a DAG for Each Transcript

The prompt’s key elements are as follows:

  1. 1.
    Core Objective. We define the primary task as constructing a compact structural causal model and a corresponding DAG that explains why an interviewee selected particular stocks over available alternatives. The prompt emphasizes identifying genuine underlying causal mechanisms rather than correlations, associations, or proxy indicators.
  2. 2.
    Input. The model receives the investor’s interview transcript as input.
  3. 3.

    Method. We provide detailed modeling instructions as follows:

    1. (a)
      Target specification: The DAG must contain exactly one outcome node, which must represent the choice of specific stocks over alternatives.
    2. (b)
      Node construction: Nodes must be directly grounded in the transcript, must be clearly interpretable, and must reflect a single underlying construct.
    3. (c)

The prompt’s key elements are as follows:

  1. 1.
    Input. The model receives the names and descriptions of the original nodes (independently generated from 1,540 transcripts) together with the standardized nodes produced in the previous step.
  2. 2.
    Method. We instruct the model to perform the mapping based on node descriptions, matching nodes only when they represent the same underlying construct or conceptual variable.

texts.title: Bottom-Up Mechanism Generation
texts.html:
The key elements of the prompt used for bottom-up mechanism generation (Section 3.3 of the main paper) are as follows:

  1. 1.
    Core Objective. The goal is to identify the key causal mechanisms that drive the stock-purchase decisions of individual investors in the 1,540 investor-level DAGs and to synthesize a general statement describing each mechanism.
  2. 2.
    Input. The model receives as input a JSON file containing the 1,540 investor DAGs constructed in the argument map construction stage (Online Appendix C.1).
  3. 3.

    Method. We provide a set of instructions as follows:

    1. (a)
      Parse all DAGs: Read all 1,540 DAGs, extract all directed paths leading to the buy-stock action, and identify recurring pathway patterns.
    2. (b)
      Identify mechanisms: Synthesize candidate mechanisms from the recurring pathways, focusing on decision rules, initiating drivers, and accelerators or moderators. The instruction emphasizes identifying true causal drivers. To maintain generality, we instruct the model to avoid splitting mechanisms based on minor variations when the core causal structure is identical, and to exclude highly idiosyncratic patterns that appear only in a small number of DAGs. To prevent hallucination, the model must tie each mechanism to the raw evidence by listing representative paths with exact node names and the IDs of supporting investors.
    3. (c)
      Write statements: Formulate a theory-like statement for each identified mechanism.

texts.title: Validation, Refinement, and Final Scoring
texts.html:
This stage uses two prompts. The validation prompt measures residual scores, which quantify how much investor behavior remains unexplained by the existing mechanisms, and extracts any unexplained patterns. The refinement prompt refines the existing mechanism set based on the validation results. We also use the validation prompt to assign the final mechanism scores (Online Appendix C.3.3).

C.3.1 Validation

The key elements of the prompt used for validation (Section 3.3 of the main paper) are as follows:

  1. 1.
    Core Objective. We task the model with assessing the residual score, that is, the degree to which the investor’s behavior remains unexplained after incorporating all mechanisms, and extracting any residual patterns.
  2. 2.
    Input. The model receives three inputs: (i) the mechanism set generated in the bottom-up mechanism generation stage (Online Appendix C.2); (ii) an individual investor’s DAG; and (iii) the corresponding interview transcript.
  3. 3.

    Method. We organize the evaluation process as follows:

    1. (a)
      Parse the investor DAG: The model reads the DAG and records all directed pathways culminating in the buy-stock action.
    2. (b)
      Score each mechanism independently: For each mechanism, the model (i) reviews the mechanism’s statement and underlying logic, (ii) evaluates whether it explains the recorded pathways, and (iii) assigns a score from 1 to 4 using the provided rubric. We require internal reasoning before scoring. A score of 4 indicates that the mechanism explains the primary driver, 3 meaningful but secondary explanatory power, 2 only fragmentary presence, and 1 absence or contradiction of the core logic of the mechanism.
    3. (c)
      Identify unexplained behavior (residual): After scoring all mechanisms, the model identifies any key pathways not explained by mechanisms scored 3 or 4 and assigns a residual score using a separate rubric. A score of 4 indicates that most central pathways remain unexplained, 3 substantial gaps, 2 only minor gaps, and 1 minimal or no residual.
    4. (d)
      Record unexplained behavior: If the residual score is 3 or 4, the model records the unexplained pathways as residual patterns.

C.3.2 Refinement

The key elements of the prompt used for refining the mechanism set based on the validation results (the refinement step in Section 3.3 of the main paper) are as follows:

  1. 1.
    Core Objective. We task the model with refining the mechanism set that describes investor stock-purchase behavior.
  2. 2.
    Input. The model receives two inputs: (i) the existing set of mechanisms, including their theoretical statements and elements, generated in Online Appendix C.2; and (ii) the residual patterns detected during validation.
  3. 3.
    Method. We instruct the model to refine the mechanism set by (i) conservatively generalizing the theoretical statements of existing mechanisms to incorporate residual patterns while preserving their core causal structure; and (ii) if substantial unexplained patterns remain, proposing at most one new mechanism derived from the dominant residual cluster.

We apply the validation and refinement prompts iteratively. The cycle repeats until fewer than 5% of the DAGs exhibit substantial unexplained residual patterns, the stopping rule described in Section 3.3 of the main paper. In our application, a single cycle meets this rule. After this cycle, 4.8% of the DAGs receive a residual score of at least 3 and 0.5% receive a residual score of 4.

C.3.3 Final Scoring

The final scoring stage (Section 3.3 of the main paper) does not involve a separate prompt. Once the mechanism set is finalized, we re-run the validation prompt described in Online Appendix C.3.1, holding the mechanism set fixed, and retain the mechanism scores it assigns. For robustness, we run the prompt fifteen times independently for each transcript and take the median score across the fifteen runs as the final score for each transcript–mechanism pair.6 The resulting output is the 1,540×13 matrix of mechanism scores used in the main analyses.

texts.title: Questionnaire
texts.html:
After completing the transcript analysis described in Section 3.3 of the main paper, we re-contact the 1,540 investors who participated in the AI interview and administer a closed-ended follow-up survey (Section 3.4 of the main paper).

We personalize the questionnaire based on the heuristics that we identify from each respondent’s interview transcript (the respondent’s “recorded approaches”). Throughout the survey, we refer to heuristics as “approaches” and, for readability, give them plain-language labels, listed below with the corresponding heuristic name in parentheses: Growth Potential (Growth/Innovation), Familiarity/Brand Trust (Familiarity/Brand Affect), Established Companies (Blue-Chip Comfort), Expert Recommendations (Authority-Follow), Price Momentum (Momentum), Multiple Signals Alignment (Confluence), Dividend Income (Dividends), Peer Influence (Social-Copy), Valuation (Undervalued Stocks) (Valuation/Mispricing), Buying the Dip (Buy-the-Dip), and ESG/Personal-values-based Investing (ESG/Values). The labels Fundamental Strength and Technical Analysis are unchanged. Each approach is accompanied by a one-sentence description. Item 6 below reproduces these descriptions in full.

Respondents complete the survey in their preferred language (English, French, German, Japanese, or Korean). For brevity, we reproduce only the English version here. Some questions depend on the respondent’s recorded approaches and on answers given earlier in the survey. Display conditions and format notes are given in italics below. They are shown here for context only and do not appear in the survey itself. The shaded boxes do not appear in the survey either. They point to the figures in Online Appendix D.2 that report the responses. The full set of survey questions follows.

  1. 1.
    In our previous interview, we discussed several approaches you use when deciding which stocks to buy. Below are the approaches we recorded for you. Please review them and answer the question that follows.
    (A table lists the respondent’s recorded approaches, each with a first-person version of its description, e.g., “Fundamental Strength: I buy companies with strong financial health, such as high profits or solid finances.”)
    Are you currently using these approaches, and if so, for how long?
    (Asked separately for each recorded approach, as a grid.)

    • Yes – a few months
    • Yes – 1–3 years
    • Yes – more than 3 years
    • No – I used these approaches in the past but no longer use them

    Responses: Figure D1, Panel (a)

  2. 2.
    (Shown only for approaches marked “No” in the previous question.)
    When you stopped using these approaches, approximately how long had you been using them?

    • A few months
    • 1–3 years
    • More than 3 years

    Responses: Figure D1, Panel (b)

  3. 3.
    How long do you usually plan to hold an individual stock for?
    Choose one of the following answers.

    • A few days or less
    • A few weeks
    • A few months
    • 1–3 years
    • More than 3 years

    Responses: Figure D2, Panel (a)

  4. 4.
    For the approaches you use, what is the main reason you believe they work well in your country’s stock market?
    Please select at most 2 answers.

    • My own investing experience
    • People I know personally (e.g., family, friends, colleagues)
    • Professional or expert sources (e.g., journalists, analysts, financial advisors, books by industry experts)
    • Individual creators and online communities (e.g., YouTubers, X/Twitter, Reddit, investing influencers, online forums)
    • Formal education (e.g., finance/economics coursework, degree programs, professional certifications)
    • Other, please specify:

    Responses: Figure D2, Panel (b)

  5. 5.
    (Shown only to respondents with more than one recorded approach.)
    It seems that you use more than one approach. Which of the following best describes how you use these approaches?
    Choose one of the following answers.

    • I use only one approach at a time, but I switch between approaches over time depending on which one seems most appropriate.
    • I use multiple approaches at the same time.

    Responses: Figure D2, Panel (c)

  6. 6.
    Now consider several other approaches investors sometimes use to decide which stocks to buy. For each approach below, please indicate whether you have heard of it before.
    (A table lists the approaches not recorded for the respondent, each with a checkbox “I have heard of this approach,” plus “None of the above.” The approach descriptions read:)

    • Fundamental Strength: Buying companies with strong financial health, such as high profits or solid finances.
    • Growth Potential: Buying companies that have the potential to grow a lot because of innovative products or services.
    • Familiarity/Brand Trust: Buying companies one knows well or trusts because of personal familiarity or brand recognition.
    • Established Companies: Preferring large, well-established companies that feel stable and reliable.
    • Expert Recommendations: Buying based on recommendations from trusted experts, advisors, or investment platforms.
    • Price Momentum: Buying stocks whose prices have been rising, expecting the trend to continue.
    • Multiple Signals Alignment: Buying only when several different sources or opinions all point in the same direction.
    • Dividend Income: Buying stocks that provide reliable and attractive dividend income.
    • Peer Influence: Buying stocks recommended or owned by trusted people, such as friends or family.
    • Valuation (Undervalued Stocks): Buying stocks that look cheap compared to what one thinks they are really worth.
    • Buying the Dip: Buying after a price drop believed to be temporary.
    • ESG/Personal-values-based Investing: Buying companies that match one’s ethical, social, or environmental values.
    • Technical Analysis: Buying based on technical indicators or chart patterns.
    • None of the above

    Responses: Figure D3, Panel (b)

  7. 7.
    For each approach you indicated you have heard of, please check the box if you have used it in the past.
    (Lists the approaches selected in the previous question, plus “None of the above.”)

    Responses: Figure D3, Panel (c)

  8. 8.
    (Shown only if the respondent’s recorded approaches and the approaches they report having used in the past together number more than three.)
    You indicated that you currently use or previously used several approaches. Please select the three approaches you have used for the longest period of time.
    (Lists the respondent’s recorded and previously used approaches. The three selected approaches (or, for respondents with three or fewer, all recorded and previously used approaches) constitute the respondent’s “top approaches” referenced below.)

    Responses: Figure D4

  9. 9.
    For each approach below, how much work do you feel each requires?
    (Asked for each of the respondent’s top approaches, in randomized order. Hovering over an approach name displays short keyword reminders.)
    Five-point slider: 1 (Very little work) to 5 (A lot of work).

    Responses: Figure D5, Panel (a)

  10. 10.
    Investors care about different things when picking stocks. Please indicate how important each of the following four goals is to you personally.
    (The four goals are presented in randomized order.) Five-point slider: 1 (Not important at all) to 5 (Extremely important).

    • Consistent High Returns: I look for stocks that, in most cases, are likely to give me high total returns (from price gains or dividends). For example, if I hold five stocks, I would ideally want most or all of them to do well.

questions.html:
Investors care about different things when picking stocks. Please indicate how important each of the following four goals is to you personally.
(The four goals are presented in randomized order.) Five-point slider: 1 (Not important at all) to 5 (Extremely important).

  • Consistent High Returns: I look for stocks that, in most cases, are likely to give me high total returns (from price gains or dividends). For example, if I hold five stocks, I would ideally want most or all of them to do well.
  • High Upside Focus: I look for stocks that could become major winners and deliver very large gains. For example, if I hold five stocks, it is OK if most deliver only moderate returns, as long as at least one becomes a very big winner.
  • Stable Performance: I look for stocks that I expect to give stable and predictable performance.
  • Personal Values Alignment: I invest in companies that match my personal values, even if it means lower financial returns.

texts.title: Robustness to Alternative Mappings between Heuristics and Firm Characteristics
texts.title_html: Robustness to Alternative Mappings between Heuristics and Firm Characteristics
texts.html:
Our measures of heuristic effectiveness depend on the firm characteristics we assign to each heuristic in Table 5 of the main paper. Because several firm characteristics can be related to the same heuristic, these assignments involve judgment. We therefore construct alternative mappings with LLMs, recalculate heuristic effectiveness under each mapping, and repeat our main tests.

We let LLMs stand in for the investors who use each heuristic. For one heuristic at a time, an LLM chooses the firm characteristics it would use to select stocks, either as a generic retail investor or with the background of an interviewed investor who uses that heuristic. It never sees our mapping or our results. We collect 10,112 such responses from two LLMs and two prompts and combine them into two kinds of alternative mappings, a consensus mapping for each LLM and prompt that keeps the most common choices and 7,596 distinct mappings that each combine one response per heuristic. We then ask how often our main conclusions survive when we replace our mapping with each alternative. The four steps below describe the procedure in detail.

  1. 1.

    Inputs and models. We use GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5, both with high reasoning effort.7 Each call supplies the description of one heuristic from Table 3 of the main paper and a list of candidate characteristics. For each candidate, the model sees only the variable name, such as ni_be, and a definition based on JKP’s documentation of factors. JKP group their 153 factors into 13 clusters, and we draw the candidates for each heuristic from the clusters related to it. We exclude composite scores and heavily model-based measures because retail investors are unlikely to use them. For Buy-the-Dip and Dividends, whose clusters offer too few relevant candidates, we add a few closely related characteristics from the “Other Factors” list in the JKP documentation. The candidate sets are as follows.

    • For Fundamental Strength, we use the Profitability, Quality, Low Leverage, and Size clusters without the composite scores f_score, o_score, z_score, qmj, qmj_prof, qmj_growth, and qmj_safety (37 candidates).
    • For Growth/Innovation, we use the Investment, Profit Growth, and Size clusters (39 candidates).
    • For Blue-Chip Comfort, we use the Low Leverage, Low Risk, and Size clusters without the composite score z_score (33 candidates).
    • For Momentum, we use the Momentum cluster (8 candidates).
    • For Buy-the-Dip, we use the Short-Term Reversal cluster and add the past two- and three-month returns, ret_2_0 and ret_3_0 (8 candidates).
    • For Dividends, we use the four payout characteristics of the Value cluster, div12m_me, eqnpo_12m, eqnpo_me, and eqpo_me, and add the trailing one-, three-, and six-month dividend yields, div1m_me, div3m_me, and div6m_me (7 candidates).
    • For Valuation/Mispricing, we use the Value cluster without the model-based measures eq_dur and ival_me (16 candidates).

    The candidate sets span 124 distinct characteristics in the JKP global factor data and include every characteristic in our mapping.

  2. 2.
    Prompts and LLM calls. We use two prompts. Prompt A asks the model to act as a retail investor who applies the heuristic and not to invent personal characteristics. Prompt B adds the background of an investor we interviewed who adopts the heuristic, and tells the model to use this background as context for what the investor could understand and apply. Conditioning a language model on the background of real respondents brings its answers closer to those of the corresponding human subgroups (Argyle, Busby, Fulda, Gubler, Rytting, and Wingate, 2023) and diversifies them, so we can test our results on a wider range of maps. The background covers country, gender, age group, education, investment knowledge, investable assets, and risk attitude. For Prompt B, we make one call for each pair of an investor and a heuristic the investor adopts, so that the responses mirror the actual users of each heuristic. There are 2,528 such pairs, because many investors adopt more than one.8 We make the same number of Prompt A calls for each heuristic. Each LLM therefore answers 2,528 calls per prompt, for 10,112 responses in total. Every call starts a new independent session. The instructions tell the model to base its choice only on the supplied information, without outside information or prior knowledge.
  3. 3.
    Responses and maps. Each response selects one to three characteristics, each of which can be used to screen or rank stocks for the heuristic. Combining one response from each of the seven heuristics in every possible way, we get 144, 360, 2,340, and 5,616 distinct maps for GPT Prompt A, GPT Prompt B, Claude Prompt A, and Claude Prompt B, respectively, and 7,596 distinct maps across the four setups. We count each distinct map once, however often the LLMs propose it, because our goal is to examine how much our findings depend on which plausible mapping a researcher might adopt. To summarize the typical choices of each LLM and prompt, we also form a consensus map that keeps, for each heuristic, the characteristics the responses select most often. We provide the four consensus mappings in Table E1.
  4. 4.
    Repeating tests. For each distinct map, we recalculate heuristic effectiveness and rerun the main tests exactly as in the main paper.

In Figure E1, we compare the estimates under every possible map with those under our mapping. Every map yields positive belief-accuracy slopes and positive historical delivery, whereas the objective-specific out-of-sample estimates spread more widely and fall below zero for a few maps. In Figure E2, we show the corresponding p-values. Apart from the returns slope of belief accuracy, which is not significant under our mapping either, p-values exceed 0.10 only for the out-of-sample tests for returns and stability, and only under some maps.

In Table E2, we report the percentage of distinct maps in each setup that support each main-paper result, which shows how sensitive our results are to the choice of map. A map supports a result if its estimate matches the corresponding main-paper estimate in sign and in statistical significance at the 10% level. A map also supports a result if its estimate favors our hypothesis more strongly by being significantly positive where the main-paper estimate is positive but not significant.

For belief accuracy and historical delivery, every map supports the pooled result and the result for each objective. In 640 of the 7,596 maps, the returns slope of belief accuracy even becomes significant. Out-of-sample delivery depends more on the mapping. Every map supports the pooled and upside results, whereas, depending on the setup, 83% to 100% of the maps support the returns result and 58% to 89% support the stability result. In the remaining maps, the estimate is positive but not significant, except in 79 Claude-based maps, where it is negative but not significant. Thus, belief accuracy, historical delivery, and pooled out-of-sample delivery do not depend on our choice of characteristics, whereas out-of-sample delivery for returns and especially stability is more sensitive to it.

parts.note_text: This figure shows how effective the follow-up survey respondents believe each of the thirteen heuristics to be. On a five-point scale from 1 (“not effective at all”) to 5 (“extremely effective”), respondents rate how effective a heuristic is at finding stocks that match an investment objective in their own local stock market. The rated heuristics are those we identify in the interview of the respondent plus any others the respondent reports having used in the past. When these exceed three, the respondent rates only the three longest-used. We elicit ratings only for the objectives the respondent rates 4 or 5 in importance, so every rating comes from a respondent who has used the heuristic and considers the objective important. Twenty-one respondents rate no objective that highly and therefore rate no heuristic. The figure pools the four objectives. Because a respondent rates between one and four objectives, we first average the ratings of each respondent for a heuristic across the objectives she rates and then average across respondents, so that each respondent counts equally. Markers report these means and horizontal bars the associated 95% confidence intervals, and we truncate the horizontal axis to the range of the estimates. All thirteen means lie above the midpoint of the scale. The number of respondents behind a heuristic ranges from 25 to 263. We order heuristics from top to bottom by their prevalence in the full interview sample.

parts.note_text:
This table examines whether investors adopt the heuristics they perceive as effective for the objectives they consider important, re-estimating the linear probability models of Table 6 of the main paper as fixed-effects logit models. We estimate the following logit counterpart of equation (1) of the main paper:

Pr (D(Adoption)ih = 1) = Λ (β1 (θig × ηPihg) + β2 ηPihg + β3 θig + αi),

in which Λ(·) denotes the logistic function, and the dependent variable, D(Adoption)ih, equals one if heuristic h is among those we identify in the interview of investor i. The key independent variable is the interaction θig × ηPihg, printed as Objective importance × Perceived effectiveness, in which θig is the five-point importance rating investor i gives to objective g, and ηPihg is the five-point rating she gives to how effective heuristic h is at finding stocks that match the objective in her own local stock market. We standardize both variables within investor, as in Table 6 of the main paper. The starting sample is that of Table 6 of the main paper, 3,744 investor–heuristic–objective observations from 572 investors. The logit estimation drops fixed-effect groups without variation in the outcome, because the group effect fits their observations perfectly, which leaves 3,291, 3,291, and 3,181 observations in Columns (1) through (3), respectively. Coefficients are in log-odds and are therefore not directly comparable in scale to the linear probability estimates. The row Pseudo R² reports McFadden’s pseudo-R², computed against an intercept-only logit on the estimation sample of each column. Investor FE, Investor × Objective FE, and Country × Heuristic × Objective FE refer to the corresponding fixed effects. We cluster standard errors at the investor level and report them in parentheses. Statistical significance at the 10%, 5%, and 1% levels is denoted by *, **, and ***, respectively.

parts.note_text: This table repeats the analysis of Table 8 of the main paper over post-adoption periods based on reported use durations. For each adopted heuristic, we use the duration of current use or, if the investor has stopped using it, the duration before stopping. We exclude investor–heuristic pairs that report a few months or an unknown duration. Taking June 30, 2026 as the common reference date, we use minimum durations of one and three years for reports of one to three years and more than three years, respectively. Monthly portfolio sorts therefore begin in July 2025 or July 2023, and we measure delivery over the month following each sort. Outcomes cover August through December 2025 (five months) or August 2023 through December 2025 (29 months, the longest period). The average period is approximately 20 months per investor, with retained heuristics weighted equally within each investor. We evaluate the choices recorded in the interviews through December 2025, including heuristics no longer used. For returns, we calculate the CAPM alpha with market betas fixed at their heuristic–country estimates from July 2013 through June 2023 portfolio sorts. For upside and stability, we use the top-1% hit-rate spread and the sign-reversed total return volatility spread. We standardize outcomes in both periods using the within-objective means and sample standard deviations across the seventy heuristic–country pairs in the 29-month window. Prioritized objectives and aggregation are otherwise as in Table 8 of the main paper. The two benchmark rows replace the retained adopted set of each investor with an equally sized random draw without replacement from (i) the covered heuristics she did not adopt in the interview (Alternative heuristics) and (ii) all seven covered heuristics (Randomly selected heuristics). The first pool also excludes adopted heuristics dropped by the duration filter. We randomly assign the drawn heuristics to the periods of the adopted heuristics and evaluate them in the same country on the same prioritized objectives. These two rows report means across 10,000 draws, with standard deviations across draws in parentheses, and their p-values are the one-sided fraction of draws that deliver at least as much as the adopted set. The sample comprises 371 investors and 621 retained investor–heuristic pairs. The columns Returns, Upside, and Stability use 180, 137, and 224 of these investors, respectively. Interpreting these results as post-adoption delivery assumes that the reported durations identify the start of use and that the reported priorities apply during the evaluation period. Statistical significance at the 10%, 5%, and 1% levels is denoted by *, **, and ***, respectively, referring to the p-values in the brackets.

parts.note_text: This table examines whether investors are more likely to adopt heuristics that are historically more effective, in their own country, for the objectives they consider important. It re-estimates the adoption regression of Table 6 of the main paper in reduced form, replacing perceived effectiveness ηPihg with historical effectiveness ηHhgc. Because we estimate historical effectiveness from archival data alone (Section 5.3 of the main paper), survey answers cannot affect it, and the estimates are immune to ex-post rationalization of one’s own choices. The dependent variable, D(Adoption), is a dummy variable equal to one if the heuristic is among those we identify in the interview of the investor. The key independent variable is the interaction Objective importance × Historical effectiveness, in which Objective importance is the five-point importance rating the investor gives to the objective, standardized within investor across the three financial objectives, and Historical effectiveness is the delivery of the heuristic on the objective in the country of the investor, estimated for the period running from July 2015 through June 2025, the ten years preceding our interviews, and standardized within objective across the seventy heuristic–country pairs. Because the analysis requires no effectiveness rating, the sample is the full grid of the 600 follow-up respondents, the seven heuristics covered by archival data, and the three financial objectives (12,600 observations), without any conditioning on which heuristics an investor rates. Investor FE, Investor × Objective FE, and Country × Heuristic × Objective FE refer to the corresponding fixed effects. We cluster standard errors at the country level and report them in parentheses. Given the small number of clusters (ten), we base the stars in Columns (1) and (2) on wild-cluster bootstrap p-values (Webb six-point weights, 9,999 replications). In Column (3), the bootstrap is not computable under the high-dimensional fixed effects, so we base the stars on the country-clustered standard errors. The interaction remains significant at the 1% level when we instead cluster standard errors at the investor level. Statistical significance at the 10%, 5%, and 1% levels is denoted by *, **, and ***, respectively.
